question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

 

EMACIATED
option_1: Robust
option_2: Plump
option_3: Gaunt
option_4: Sturdy
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Gaunt.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Emaciated (adjective) means abnormally thin and weak, usually from hunger or long illness. (अत्यंत दुर्बल, कृशकाय)
◦ Example: The rescued cattle were emaciated after weeks without fodder.

 

• Gaunt carries the same sense — lean, bony and haggard in appearance. (कृशकाय, अस्थिपंजर-सा)
◦ Example: His gaunt face showed how hard the winter had been.

 

• The word comes from Latin macer, 'thin' — the same root as meagre, which is a useful hook for remembering it.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Robust (हृष्ट-पुष्ट): strong and healthy — an antonym.

 

• Option 2: Plump (मोटा, गोल-मटोल): pleasantly fat and rounded — an antonym.

 

• Option 4: Sturdy (मजबूत, बलिष्ठ): solidly built and vigorous — an antonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Other synonyms of emaciated: haggard, wasted, skeletal, cadaverous, scrawny.

 

• Distinguish emaciated (thin from illness or hunger) from slender or slim, which are complimentary words for a naturally graceful build.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

 

VACILLATE
option_1: Waver
option_2: Persist
option_3: Resolve
option_4: Persevere
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Waver.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Vacillate (verb) means to keep changing one's mind; to be unable to decide between two courses. (हिचकिचाना, दुविधा में रहना)
◦ Example: The board vacillated for months before approving the plan.

 

• Waver means exactly this — to hesitate and swing between two opinions or intentions. (डगमगाना, अनिश्चित होना)
◦ Example: His confidence began to waver as the questions grew harder.

 

• The word comes from Latin vacillare, 'to sway'; the physical image of swaying to and fro underlies the mental sense.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: Persist (डटे रहना): to continue firmly in a course of action — an antonym.

 

• Option 3: Resolve (दृढ़ निश्चय करना): to decide firmly — an antonym.

 

• Option 4: Persevere (लगे रहना): to keep on in spite of difficulty — an antonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Other synonyms of vacillate: dither, waffle, oscillate, falter, shilly-shally.

 

• The noun is vacillation, and the adjective vacillating — both common in official and editorial English.

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

 

MAGNANIMOUS
option_1: Generous
option_2: Liberal
option_3: Benevolent
option_4: Petty
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Petty.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Magnanimous (adjective) means generous and forgiving, especially towards a rival or a defeated opponent; noble in spirit. (उदार, उदारचित्त, महामना)
◦ Example: He was magnanimous in victory and praised the losing side warmly.

 

• Its opposite is petty — small-minded; preoccupied with trifles and unwilling to overlook them. (क्षुद्र, ओछा)
◦ Example: The dispute was kept alive by petty objections on both sides.

 

• Options 1, 2 and 3 all denote generosity, so they are synonyms of the given word and may be eliminated as a group.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Generous (उदार): willing to give freely — a synonym.

 

• Option 2: Liberal (मुक्तहस्त, उदारमना): giving freely; broad-minded — a synonym.

 

• Option 3: Benevolent (परोपकारी): well-meaning and kindly — a synonym.

 

NOTE

 

• The word is built from Latin magnus ('great') and animus ('spirit') — literally 'great-souled'. The noun is magnanimity.

 

• Other antonyms: mean, miserly, vindictive, small-minded, ungenerous.

question:
Choose the correct meaning of the given idiom.

 

A red herring
option_1: A rare and valuable discovery
option_2: A misleading clue that draws attention away from the real issue
option_3: A sudden outburst of anger
option_4: An ally who arrives unexpectedly
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. A misleading clue that draws attention away from the real issue.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• 'A red herring' means something introduced into a discussion or investigation that distracts attention from the real question. (ध्यान भटकाने वाली बात)
◦ Example: The argument about the committee's name was a red herring that delayed the real decision.

 

• The phrase comes from the strong-smelling smoked herring, which turns reddish-brown when cured and was said to be used to lay a false trail across the scent of a hunted animal.

 

• The essential idea is therefore distraction, and usually deliberate distraction — which none of the other options conveys.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 would suit an expression such as 'a windfall' or 'a find'.

 

• Option 3 describes anger, for which the idiom is 'to fly off the handle'.

 

• Option 4 has no connection with the phrase.

 

NOTE

 

• Related idioms of misdirection: to throw dust in someone's eyes, a wild goose chase, to lead someone up the garden path, a smokescreen.

question: Choose the correct spelling of a word meaning 'to give up a claim, right or possession formally'.
option_1: Relinquish
option_2: Relinqish
option_3: Relinquesh
option_4: Relinquich
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Relinquish.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Relinquish (verb) means to give up or surrender something formally — a right, a claim, a post or a possession. (त्याग देना, छोड़ देना)
◦ Example: He relinquished his claim to the property in favour of his sister.

 

• The correct division is RE - LIN - QUISH. Two points settle the question:
◦ the q must be followed by u, as it almost always is in English;
◦ the ending is -ish, not -esh or -ich.

 

• It comes from Latin relinquere, 'to leave behind' — the same root as relic and derelict.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: Relinqish — wrong; the u after q has been dropped.

 

• Option 3: Relinquesh — wrong; the vowel of the last syllable is i, not e.

 

• Option 4: Relinquich — wrong; the ending -ish has been written -ich.

 

NOTE

 

• Synonyms: surrender, renounce, forgo, cede, waive, abandon. Antonyms: retain, keep, claim, assert.

question: Find the correctly spelled word meaning 'behaving as though one were superior to others'.
option_1: Supersilious
option_2: Superscilious
option_3: Supercillious
option_4: Supercilious
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Supercilious.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Supercilious (adjective) means behaving with haughty contempt, as if one were better than everybody else. (घमंडी, तिरस्कारपूर्ण)
◦ Example: The clerk answered every query in the same supercilious tone.

 

• The correct division is SU - PER - CI - LI - OUS. Three points decide it:
◦ the third letter group is -ci-, spelt with c, never s;
◦ the l is single, not doubled;
◦ there is no s after 'super-'.

 

• The word comes from Latin supercilium, 'eyebrow' — the raised eyebrow being the classic gesture of disdain.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Supersilious — wrong; the c has been replaced by s.

 

• Option 2: Superscilious — wrong; an intrusive s has been inserted after 'super-'.

 

• Option 3: Supercillious — wrong; the l has been needlessly doubled.

 

NOTE

 

• Synonyms: haughty, disdainful, arrogant, condescending, imperious. Antonyms: humble, modest, unassuming, deferential.

question: Choose the correct one-word substitute for: 'A speech delivered without any previous preparation'.
option_1: Soliloquy
option_2: Extempore
option_3: Monologue
option_4: Recitation
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Extempore.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Extempore means spoken or done on the spur of the moment, without notes or rehearsal. (तत्काल, बिना तैयारी का)
◦ Example: Asked to speak at short notice, she delivered a fluent extempore address.

 

• The word comes from Latin ex tempore, 'out of the time' — that is, arising from the moment itself. The synonym impromptu carries the same sense.

 

• The other three options all name kinds of speech, but each is defined by who is speaking or what is spoken, not by the absence of preparation — which is the whole point of the definition.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Soliloquy (आत्मभाषण): a speech in which a character, alone on stage, speaks his thoughts aloud.

 

• Option 3: Monologue (एकालाप): a long speech by one person in a conversation or performance.

 

• Option 4: Recitation (आवृत्ति, पाठ): the delivery aloud of something already learnt by heart — the exact opposite of unprepared.

 

NOTE

 

• Note the useful contrast: a soliloquy is addressed to nobody, a monologue is addressed to an audience, and a dialogue requires two or more speakers.

question: Choose the correct one-word substitute for: 'A list of the books and articles referred to in a scholarly work'.
option_1: Biography
option_2: Anthology
option_3: Bibliography
option_4: Glossary
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Bibliography.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A bibliography is a list of the books, papers and other sources consulted or cited in a piece of writing. (संदर्भ-ग्रंथ सूची)
◦ Example: The thesis ran to two hundred pages, with a bibliography of sixty titles.

 

• The word joins Greek biblion ('book') and graphia ('writing'). The same root biblio- gives bibliophile (a lover of books) and bibliotheca (a library).

 

• All four options name kinds of written compilation, so the answer turns on what is compiled.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Biography (जीवनी): an account of a person's life written by somebody else.

 

• Option 2: Anthology (संकलन): a collection of poems, essays or stories by various authors.

 

• Option 4: Glossary (कठिन शब्दों की अर्थ-सूची): an alphabetical list of difficult terms with their explanations, usually at the end of a book.

 

NOTE

 

• Complete the set for the exam: autobiography (a life written by its own subject), memoir (recollections of part of a life), index (an alphabetical list of topics with page numbers), appendix (supplementary matter at the end).

question:
Fill in the blank with the correct option:

 

The soup tastes _____ even though no salt has been added to it.
option_1: well
option_2: good
option_3: nicely
option_4: goodly
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. good.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Taste here is a linking verb (also called a copula), like be, seem, appear, look, sound, smell, feel and become. A linking verb is followed by an adjective, not an adverb, because the word describes the subject and not the action.
◦ Example: The rose smells sweet (not 'sweetly'); the music sounds beautiful (not 'beautifully').

 

• The sentence therefore requires the adjective good, which describes the soup: The soup tastes good.

 

• Well is an adverb of manner and would wrongly describe how the soup performs the act of tasting — a meaning the sentence does not intend.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: well — an adverb; correct after an ordinary action verb, as in *She sings well*.

 

• Option 3: nicely — likewise an adverb, and unidiomatic after 'taste'.

 

• Option 4: goodly — an archaic adjective meaning 'considerable in size', as in 'a goodly sum'; it is not the adverb of 'good'.

 

NOTE

 

• Well is an adjective only when it refers to health — *He is not well today*. Wherever the choice lies between good and well after a linking verb, good is the form required.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The committee emphasised on the need (1)/ for stricter monitoring (2)/ of the funds released (3)/ to the district offices. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (1).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Emphasise is a transitive verb: it takes a direct object and needs no preposition after it. 'Emphasised on the need' is therefore wrong.

 

• Part (1) must read 'The committee emphasised the need'. If a preposition is wanted, the noun form must be used instead — *laid emphasis on the need*.

 

• The corrected sentence: The committee emphasised the need for stricter monitoring of the funds released to the district offices.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (2) is correct — need for is the right collocation.

 

• Part (3) and Part (4) are sound; released to correctly names the recipient.

 

NOTE

 

• Other verbs that take no preposition although one is commonly added in Indian English: discuss (about), comprise (of), order (for), request (for), resemble (to), accompany (with — say 'accompanied by' of a person), reach (at), enter (into a room), attack (on).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

Between you and I, (1)/ the decision to shift the office (2)/ had been taken long before (3)/ the notice was circulated. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (1).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Between is a preposition, and a pronoun that follows a preposition must be in the objective case. The objective form of I is me.

 

• Part (1) must therefore read 'Between you and me'. The presence of another word joined by 'and' does not change the rule — remove it and the ear settles the matter at once: nobody says 'between I'.

 

• The corrected sentence: Between you and me, the decision to shift the office had been taken long before the notice was circulated.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (3) is correct — the past perfect had been taken properly shows the earlier of two past events.

 

• Part (2) and Part (4) are sound.

 

NOTE

 

• The same rule governs 'let you and me', 'between him and me', 'for you and me'. The reverse error also occurs — *He gave it to my brother and I* should be *to my brother and me*.

question:
Change the following from active to passive.

 

The guards made the visitors wait outside the gate.
option_1: The visitors were made wait outside the gate by the guards.
option_2: The visitors had been made wait outside the gate by the guards.
option_3: The visitors were make to wait outside the gate by the guards.
option_4: The visitors were made to wait outside the gate by the guards.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. The visitors were made to wait outside the gate by the guards.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The verb make, in the causative sense of 'compel', is followed in the active voice by a bare infinitive — *made the visitors wait*.

 

• In the passive, however, the to reappears: be made + to + infinitive.
◦ Active: They made him sign the form. → Passive: He was made to sign the form.

 

• Applying this here: made the visitors wait → were made to wait, with the guards becoming the agent after by. The simple past is retained throughout.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 omits the to, which the passive of 'make' requires.

 

• Option 2 shifts the tense to the past perfect and also drops the to.

 

• Option 3 uses the base form make instead of the past participle made.

 

NOTE

 

• The same behaviour is seen with see, hear and watch: *They saw him enter* becomes *He was seen to enter*. Note the exception — let does not follow this pattern; its passive is normally formed with be allowed to.

question:
Convert the sentence provided below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure.

 

The parcel was delivered by the courier this morning.
option_1: The courier delivers the parcel this morning.
option_2: The courier was delivering the parcel this morning.
option_3: The courier had delivered the parcel this morning.
option_4: The courier delivered the parcel this morning.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. The courier delivered the parcel this morning.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The given sentence is in the simple past passive — was delivered. Its active counterpart must also be in the simple past.

 

• Steps applied here:
◦ The agent the courier becomes the subject.
◦ was delivered → delivered.
◦ The parcel becomes the object, and the by-phrase is dropped.

 

• The time expression this morning stays where it is and confirms that the past tense must be kept.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 shifts the sentence into the simple present.

 

• Option 2 substitutes the past continuous, turning a completed delivery into an action in progress.

 

• Option 3 gives the past perfect, which would require a second, later past event to relate to.

 

NOTE

 

• In converting a passive to an active, always ask three questions in order: who is the agent (that becomes the subject), what is the tense (that must not change), and what was the original subject (that becomes the object).

question:
Select the sentence containing the homonym of the highlighted word.

 

The capital of the state was shifted to a new site in 1960.
option_1: The new capital was planned by a French architect.
option_2: The firm needs fresh capital before it can expand the plant.
option_3: Delegates from every district arrived in the capital for the summit.
option_4: The road linking the capital to the port was widened last year.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The firm needs fresh capital before it can expand the plant.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A homonym is a word identical in spelling and pronunciation to another but carrying an entirely different meaning. (समनामी शब्द)

 

• In the given sentence capital means the city that is the seat of government of a state or country. The question therefore asks for the sentence in which the same word carries a different meaning.

 

• Option 2 uses capital to mean wealth or funds available for investment in a business. The words 'firm', 'fresh' and 'expand the plant' fix this financial sense beyond doubt.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1, Option 3 and Option 4 all use capital in the same geographical sense as the highlighted word, so none of them qualifies as a homonym.

 

• Capital has further senses worth knowing: an upper-case letter (a capital A), the top of a pillar in architecture, and the adjective in capital punishment.

 

NOTE

 

• Keep the three terms distinct: homonyms are alike in spelling and sound (capital, pupil, stern); homophones sound alike but are spelt differently (capital/capitol, sight/site); homographs are spelt alike but may be pronounced differently (lead, tear, row).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The older clerks found it hard to cope up with the new software.
option_1: coping with
option_2: cope up
option_3: cope with
option_4: cope up against
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. cope with.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The verb cope is followed directly by with and by nothing else. 'Cope up with' is a very common Indian-English error produced by confusion with 'keep up with'. (सामना करना, निभा लेना)
◦ Example: She coped with the extra workload without complaint.

 

• The corrected sentence: The older clerks found it hard to cope with the new software.

 

• Note that after hard to the verb must remain in the base form — 'to cope', not 'to coping'.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: coping with — the preposition is right, but the -ing form cannot follow 'hard to'.

 

• Option 2: cope up — retains the intrusive up and drops the necessary with.

 

• Option 4: cope up against — compounds the intrusive up with a wrong preposition.

 

NOTE

 

• Compare the two verbs that are confused here: cope with a difficulty, but keep up with a person or a pace. Similar traps: discuss (not 'discuss about'), comprise (not 'comprise of'), stress (not 'stress on').

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

A city is judged by its buildings, but it is lived in through the spaces between them. The footpath, the maidan, the shaded bus stop and the step of a public tank are where most urban life actually happens, and they are also the parts of a city that are surrendered first. What replaces them is rarely announced as a loss; it arrives as parking, as widening, as beautification.

 

The footpath is the clearest case. Where it survives at all it is treated as residual space — the strip left over after the carriageway has taken what it needs — and it is then further reduced by transformer boxes, hoardings and parked two-wheelers. A pedestrian in most Indian cities walks not on a path but between obstructions, and the design of the road announces, more honestly than any policy document, whose convenience the city was built around.

 

Less obvious is what may be called hostile design: the bench divided by armrests so that nobody can lie along it, the ledge studded so that nobody can sit on it, the shelter with no seat at all. Such details are seldom debated, because each is trivial by itself and none is presented as an exclusion. Their effect is nonetheless cumulative, and it falls hardest on those with nowhere else to go — the vendor between customers, the labourer waiting for work, the old man who cannot walk to the next park.

 

Public space is also where a city's inequalities become visible, which is one reason its decline is tolerated. A household with a lawn does not need a maidan; a family with a car does not need a shaded footpath. Those who can purchase private substitutes withdraw from the shared version and then, quite reasonably from their own point of view, cease to defend it. The commons decays not because it is attacked but because it is abandoned by the people best able to protect it.

 

The remedies are neither expensive nor mysterious: a continuous footpath, a tree every few metres, a bench without armrests, a tap that works. What is missing is not money or expertise but the conviction that the street belongs to everyone who uses it. Until that conviction returns, a city will keep producing handsome buildings that nobody can comfortably walk between.

 

What does the author mean by 'hostile design'?
option_1: Street fittings shaped so that they cannot be sat or lain on.
option_2: Buildings deliberately made ugly to discourage visitors.
option_3: Road layouts designed to slow down motor traffic.
option_4: Architecture that ignores the climate of the region.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Street fittings shaped so that they cannot be sat or lain on.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage defines the term by example immediately after naming it: 'the bench divided by armrests so that nobody can lie along it, the ledge studded so that nobody can sit on it, the shelter with no seat at all.'

 

• The common feature of all three is that an ordinary piece of street furniture has been shaped to prevent a particular use, which is exactly what Option 1 states.

 

• The author's point is that the exclusion is deliberate but unannounced: such details are 'seldom debated, because each is trivial by itself and none is presented as an exclusion.'

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 reads 'hostile' as ugliness, whereas the passage is about function, not appearance.

 

• Option 3 describes traffic calming, which the passage never mentions.

 

• Option 4 introduces climate, a matter outside this paragraph.

 

NOTE

 

• When a passage coins or borrows a term and follows it with a colon or a dash, the words after that mark are the definition — and usually the wording of the correct option.

According to the passage, how is the footpath treated in most Indian cities?
option_1: As residual space left over after the carriageway has taken what it needs.
option_2: As the first element to be planned in a new road.
option_3: As a protected area from which vehicles are strictly excluded.
option_4: As the responsibility of the residents rather than of the municipality.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. As residual space left over after the carriageway has taken what it needs.

• The passage says the footpath 'is treated as residual space — the strip left over after the carriageway has taken what it needs', and that it is then further reduced by transformer boxes, hoardings and parked two-wheelers.

 

• The consequence is stated in the next sentence: a pedestrian 'walks not on a path but between obstructions'.

 

• The author then draws the inference that the design of the road shows 'whose convenience the city was built around' — that is, the motorist's.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 reverses the passage; the footpath is what is left after the road has been planned.

 

• Option 3 is contradicted by the reference to parked two-wheelers on the footpath.

 

• Option 4 introduces a question of municipal responsibility that the passage does not raise.

 

NOTE

 

• Note the author's phrase 'more honestly than any policy document' — a hint that the passage is contrasting stated policy with actual practice.

Their effect is nonetheless cumulative, and it falls hardest on those with nowhere else to go — the vendor between customers, the labourer waiting for work, the old man who cannot walk to the next park.

 

Public space is also where a city's inequalities become visible, which is one reason its decline is tolerated. A household with a lawn does not need a maidan; a family with a car does not need a shaded footpath. Those who can purchase private substitutes withdraw from the shared version and then, quite reasonably from their own point of view, cease to defend it. The commons decays not because it is attacked but because it is abandoned by the people best able to protect it.

 

The remedies are neither expensive nor mysterious: a continuous footpath, a tree every few metres, a bench without armrests, a tap that works. What is missing is not money or expertise but the conviction that the street belongs to everyone who uses it. Until that conviction returns, a city will keep producing handsome buildings that nobody can comfortably walk between.

 

According to the passage, on whom does the effect of hostile design fall most heavily?
option_1: On tourists unfamiliar with the city.
option_2: On motorists looking for parking space.
option_3: On those with nowhere else to go, such as vendors and waiting labourers.
option_4: On municipal engineers who must maintain the street.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. On those with nowhere else to go, such as vendors and waiting labourers.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage states that the effect of such details 'is nonetheless cumulative, and it falls hardest on those with nowhere else to go'.

 

• It then names them: 'the vendor between customers, the labourer waiting for work, the old man who cannot walk to the next park.'

 

• The reasoning is that a person who has an alternative is not injured by a bench he cannot lie on; a person who has none is.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 introduces tourists, who are nowhere mentioned.

 

• Option 2 names the group whose convenience the passage says the city is in fact built around.

 

• Option 4 shifts the burden to municipal staff, a point the passage does not make.

 

NOTE

 

• Where a passage supplies a list of examples immediately after a general phrase, the correct option normally echoes both — the general phrase and at least one example.

What is missing is not money or expertise but the conviction that the street belongs to everyone who uses it. Until that conviction returns, a city will keep producing handsome buildings that nobody can comfortably walk between.

 

Why, according to the author, is the decline of public space tolerated?
option_1: Because most citizens are unaware that public space exists.
option_2: Because those who can buy private substitutes withdraw from the shared version and stop defending it.
option_3: Because the courts have refused to intervene in such matters.
option_4: Because maintaining public space is technically very difficult.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Because those who can buy private substitutes withdraw from the shared version and stop defending it.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage explains: 'A household with a lawn does not need a maidan; a family with a car does not need a shaded footpath.'

 

• It then states the consequence: those who can purchase private substitutes 'withdraw from the shared version and then, quite reasonably from their own point of view, cease to defend it.'

 

• The conclusion is put in a single sentence: 'The commons decays not because it is attacked but because it is abandoned by the people best able to protect it.'

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 attributes ignorance to citizens, which the passage never suggests.

 

• Option 3 brings in the courts, a subject absent from the passage.

 

• Option 4 is contradicted by the final paragraph, which calls the remedies 'neither expensive nor mysterious'.

 

NOTE

option_4: The absence of the conviction that the street belongs to everyone who uses it.

question:
A sentence is provided in direct speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding indirect speech.

 

She said to me, “Where do you keep the spare keys?”
option_1: She asked me where do I keep the spare keys.
option_2: She asked me that where I kept the spare keys.
option_3: She asked me where I kept the spare keys.
option_4: She said me where did I keep the spare keys.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. She asked me where I kept the spare keys.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The quoted sentence is a wh-interrogative. Three rules apply together:
◦ the reporting verb said to becomes asked;
◦ the question word where itself serves as the connective, so that must not be added;
◦ the interrogative order is dropped — the clause becomes a statement with the subject before the verb.

 

• Backshift also applies: do you keep (simple present) → kept (simple past), and the pronoun you becomes I.

 

• The question mark disappears, since the reported sentence is now a statement.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 keeps the interrogative order and the present tense.

 

• Option 2 wrongly inserts that before the question word; a that and a wh-word can never stand together.

 

• Option 4 uses the ungrammatical said me and retains the auxiliary did in interrogative order.

 

NOTE

 

• For yes/no questions the connective must be supplied — if or whether — because there is no question word to do the work: *He asked me whether I had finished.*

question:
A sentence is provided in direct speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding indirect speech.

 

He said, “I met her at the conference two years ago.”
option_1: He said that he met her at the conference two years ago.
option_2: He said that he had met her at the conference two years later.
option_3: He said that he has met her at the conference two years ago.
option_4: He said that he had met her at the conference two years before.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. He said that he had met her at the conference two years before.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Two separate changes are required here.
◦ The simple past (met) backshifts to the past perfect (had met) after the past reporting verb.
◦ The time expression ago, which measures backwards from the moment of speaking, becomes before (or 'earlier'), which measures backwards from the moment reported.

 

• The pronoun I becomes he, and the conjunction that is supplied.

 

• The completed sentence: He said that he had met her at the conference two years before.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 leaves both the tense and ago unchanged.

 

• Option 2 backshifts the verb correctly but replaces ago with later, reversing the direction of time.

 

• Option 3 uses the present perfect, which cannot follow a past reporting verb, and retains ago.

 

NOTE

 

• Standard time-word shifts: now → then; today → that day; tomorrow → the next day; yesterday → the previous day; ago → before; last night → the previous night; here → there; this → that.

question:
A sentence is provided in indirect speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding direct speech.

 

She said that never had she seen so grand a procession.
option_1: “Never have I seen so grand a procession,” she said.
option_2: “Never I have seen so grand a procession,” she said.
option_3: “Never had she seen so grand a procession,” she said.
option_4: “She had never seen so grand a procession,” she said.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. “Never have I seen so grand a procession,” she said.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The reported clause preserves the negative inversion that the original words carried: when a sentence opens with never, seldom, rarely, little, hardly or no sooner, the auxiliary moves before the subject.

 

• Converting back to direct speech requires two changes:
◦ the backshifted had seen reverts to the present perfect have seen;
◦ the pronoun she reverts to I, since the speaker was talking about herself.

 

• The inversion itself must be kept, because it belonged to the speaker's own words: Never have I seen ...

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 drops the inversion, giving the ungrammatical 'Never I have seen'.

 

• Option 3 retains the third-person she and the backshifted had, both of which belong to the indirect version.

 

• Option 4 removes the inversion altogether and keeps the third person.

 

NOTE

 

• Other negative adverbials that force inversion: Seldom have I ..., Rarely does he ..., Little did they know ..., Not until later did we realise ..., Under no circumstances should you ...

question:
Rearrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph:

 

1. These include the depth of the water, the shape of the coast and the pull of the moon.
2. The height of a tide at any port depends on several separate influences.
3. Tide tables are therefore prepared years in advance for each port separately.
4. Taken together they allow the height to be calculated with great precision for a given place.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. 2-1-4-3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Sentence 2 opens the paragraph: it states the general proposition and announces that several influences will follow. A sentence promising a list must precede the list.

 

• Sentence 1 supplies that list, and its opening word 'These' is a backward reference to the influences named in sentence 2.

 

• Sentence 4 follows with 'Taken together they', which can only refer to the influences just enumerated in sentence 1, and states what those influences make possible.

 

• Sentence 3 concludes, marked by 'therefore', drawing the practical consequence — that tide tables can be prepared in advance.

 

• The chain is therefore proposition → the list → what follows from the list → practical consequence: 2-1-4-3.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (1-2-4-3) opens with 'These', a demonstrative with nothing to refer back to.

 

• Option 3 (2-4-1-3) places 'Taken together they' before the items being taken together.

 

• Option 4 (4-2-1-3) begins in the middle of the argument altogether.

 

NOTE

 

• A sentence that announces a number — 'several influences', 'three stages', 'two methods' — almost always opens the paragraph, with the items following immediately.

question:
Rearrange the following sentences in correct order to make a logical passage.

 

1. It can hold several times its own weight in water.
2. Vermicompost is now widely used in kitchen gardens.
3. It is produced by earthworms feeding on decomposed organic waste.
4. Gardeners therefore find that beds treated with it need watering less often.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. 2-3-1-4.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Sentence 2 opens the paragraph: it names the subject — vermicompost — and states the general fact. No other sentence introduces the term.

 

• Sentence 3 explains how it is made, and its pronoun 'It' requires the named subject of sentence 2 immediately before it.

 

• Sentence 1 gives the property that matters for the conclusion — its capacity to hold water.

 

• Sentence 4 closes, marked by 'therefore', drawing the practical consequence of that property for the gardener.

 

• The order is therefore subject → how it is made → its property → the practical result: 2-3-1-4.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (2-1-3-4) separates the conclusion in sentence 4 from the water-holding property it depends on.

 

• Option 3 (3-2-1-4) opens with the pronoun 'It', which has no antecedent.

 

• Option 4 (1-2-3-4) likewise begins with an unattached 'It'.

 

NOTE

 

• Two rules settle most of these questions: a pronoun can never appear before the noun it stands for, and a sentence beginning therefore, hence or thus almost always closes the paragraph.
